posts.title: Generate a Component in One Command
posts.content:
# Generate a Component in One Command

Each component here is five files: the component, a barrel export (a small file that re-exports it), unit tests, a Storybook story (a live preview page) and an accessibility test. Writing those by hand invites mistakes, so the project ships a generator.

## Run it with prompts

```bash
docker compose exec grand-daze pnpm run generate:component
```

The generator asks for a name and a category, then writes all five files. It also accepts the same answers as arguments on the command-line interface (CLI, the text prompt you type commands into), which is useful when a script runs it. The panel below shows how.

<details>
<summary>CLI Arguments for Automation</summary>

**For scripting and automation:**

```bash
docker compose exec grand-daze pnpm run generate:component -- \
  --name CountdownBanner \
  --category atomic \
  --hasProps true
```

**Available categories:** `subatomic`, `atomic`, `molecular`, `organisms`, `templates`

</details>

## After it runs

Open the new folder, fill in the component and run its tests. The generated tests already pass, so a red test means something you changed.

posts.title: A Token Is an Identity: Scope One Per Automation
posts.content:
# A Token Is an Identity: Scope One Per Automation

Sooner or later something other than you needs to act on your repository: a script, a scheduled job, or an assistant in an editor such as [Cursor](https://cursor.com/). It needs credentials, and those credentials decide who [GitHub](https://github.com/) believes is acting.

> **The core idea.** A token is not a key you copy around. It is an identity. Whatever holds it acts as the person or service it was issued to.

## 🔒 The trap: sharing your own token

Handing over a copy of your Personal Access Token (PAT, a password-like string that lets software act as you) is quick. It breaks three things at once:

- **Attribution.** Every commit and issue the automation creates is recorded under your name.
- **Security.** One leaked copy exposes everything your account can reach.
- **Revocation.** You cannot cut off the automation without also cutting off yourself.

> **Short version.** Shared tokens trade five minutes of setup for a mess you cannot undo.

## Fine-Grained Tokens and Least Privilege

Least privilege means giving a task the smallest set of permissions that lets it finish. GitHub's fine-grained tokens let you choose one repository and a short list of permissions. This table shows a typical set for an automation that opens issues and pull requests.

| Permission    | Access       | Why the automation needs it                      |
| ------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Contents      | Read & write | To push a branch with its changes                |
| Pull requests | Read & write | To open the pull request and answer review notes |
| Issues        | Read & write | To open and label issues                         |
| Metadata      | Read-only    | Required by GitHub for every fine-grained token  |

> **Start from nothing.** Add a permission only when something fails without it.

> **Pick an expiry.** A token that lapses in 30 days is a token that cannot be forgotten.

> **Name it for the job.** `issue-bot-grand-daze` tells you what to revoke. `my-token` does not.

## Check who you are before you act

Before an automation does anything, confirm which identity it holds:

```bash
# Shows the account and the token's scopes
gh auth status
```

If the answer is not the identity you meant, stop and fix it. Everything that follows will be recorded under that name.

> **Check, then act.** A one-second status command is cheaper than rewriting history.

## Summary

- One token per automation, one repository per token.
- The smallest permissions that work, with an expiry date.
- Confirm the identity first.

posts.title: Review Without Rewriting
posts.content:
# Review Without Rewriting

A collaborator opens a pull request (a proposed change that waits for review before it joins the main code). You spot a problem. The quickest move is to push a fix onto their branch yourself. This post explains why that is usually the wrong move, and what to do instead.

> **Suggest, don't overwrite.** A fixup commit on their branch puts your name on their work and skips the checks they run on their own machine.

## The three approaches

The table below compares the ways a reviewer can ask for a change. Scroll sideways on a phone to see every column.

| Approach                                                        | Does the author keep credit for the change? | Does the author's own toolchain still run?                           | Good for                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| **Fixup commit** pushed to `feature/their-branch-name-here`     | No. The commit carries the reviewer's name  | No. Their pre-commit hooks never see the change                      | Almost never, for a collaborator's pull request |
| **Inline suggestion** accepted with one click                   | Yes. Accepting it commits as the author     | Partly. It lands on the branch before their local checks have run it | A truly trivial one-line typo                   |
| **Request changes** with a short note saying what to do and why | Yes. The author writes and commits the fix  | Yes. Their editor, hooks and type checks all run                     | Anything with more than one moving part         |

An inline suggestion keeps the author's name on the commit, which is the whole point of the feature. It still lands without the author's local checks, so keep it for trivia.

## Why the note matters

A bare "please fix" costs the author a round trip. A note that names the file, says what is wrong and explains the reason lets them fix it in one pass.

> **Say what and why.** "The button is 36 pixels tall, and our touch-target rule is 44" beats "make this bigger".

## When you can overrule this

Some changes belong to the reviewer: a release the author cannot cut, or a fix to the shared build. Say so in the review, so the author knows why their branch changed.

> **Tell them before it happens.** A surprise commit on your branch feels like a correction. The same commit, announced in advance, feels like help.

posts.title: Hello, world
posts.content:
# Hello, world

This is the only post a freshly rebranded fork keeps. Everything else in
`public/blog/` belongs to the template and is removed by `scripts/rebrand.sh`, because a
new project should not publish the template's posts under its own name.

Read this once, then delete it.

## How a post works

A post is one markdown file in `public/blog/`. The frontmatter above is the whole
contract:

- `title`, `date`, `excerpt` — what the blog index and the post page render.
- `slug` — the URL. It overrides the filename, so `hello-world.md` need not be
  `/blog/hello-world/`. Keep them the same unless you have a reason.
- `tags`, `categories` — the filters on the blog index.
- `featuredImage` — **what a reader sees**, on the card and at the top of the post. A
  post without one is blank on the site.
- `ogImage` — the social card, shown when someone pastes the link. Use a PNG, 1200×630.

Both images must exist on disk; a test fails the build if they do not.

## The one thing that will catch you out

`public/blog/*.md` is **not** what the site serves. The site, the sitemap, the RSS feed
and the JSON feed all read `src/lib/blog/blog-data.json`, a committed index — and
generating it is deliberately not part of the build.

So after adding, editing, **or deleting** a post:

```bash
docker compose exec grand-daze pnpm generate:blog
```

and commit the resulting `blog-data.json` diff. Skip it and nothing happens: your edit
never ships, and a deleted post stays live, still in the sitemap, still in the feed.

`scripts/__tests__/blog-index-matches-disk.test.js` fails when the two sides disagree, so
CI will tell you — but it is quicker to remember than to be told.

## Writing your own

Copy this file, change the frontmatter, replace the body, regenerate the index:

```bash
cp public/blog/hello-world.md public/blog/my-first-post.md
# edit it, then:
docker compose exec grand-daze pnpm generate:blog
```

Then delete this one.
